lal_1960.citation: B. B. Lal (1960 [published 1962]). 'From the Megalithic to the Harappa: Tracing Back the Graffiti on the Pottery'. Ancient India, No. 16, pp. 4-24.
lal_1960.author_epistemic_caution: Lal explicitly warned it would be 'presumptuous' to assign phonetic, syllabic, or alphabetic linguistic values based solely on graffiti mark overlap.
lal_1960.verbatim_verified_quote: out of the total of sixty-one symbols noted so far, as many as forty-seven are common to the megalithic pottery on the one hand and the Harappan and post-Harappan chalcolithic on the other... eighty-nine per cent of the megalithic symbols go back to the chalcolithic-Harappan times.

rajan_sivanantham_2025.citation: K. Rajan & R. Sivanantham (2025). Indus Signs and Graffiti Marks of Tamil Nadu: A Morphological Study. Department of Archaeology, Government of Tamil Nadu.
rajan_sivanantham_2025.open_dataset_availability_audit: NO official open machine-readable CSV/JSON/GitHub dataset published by TN State Dept. of Archaeology as of verification; available via Tamil Digital Library flipbook/print monograph and Harappa.com research summaries.
key_scholarly_critiques: Low geometric stroke-complexity confounder (simple lines, Vs, Xs, triangles, strokes recur independently across unrelated Bronze/Iron Age ceramic traditions worldwide).
Chronological gap between Mature Harappan urban collapse (~1900 BCE) and South Indian Iron Age / Early Historic ceramic graffiti contexts (~2nd-1st millennium BCE).
Graffiti marks are overwhelmingly isolated single/double potmarks rather than syntax-governed multi-sign sentences.

visual_verification_note: All ICIT sign IDs below were visually rendered and inspected from data/raw/sk_indus_script-webfont.ttf prior to categorization; missing-glyph (.notdef U+2047) signs such as 515 are excluded from visual-complexity modeling.

megalithic_shared_categories.shape_desc: Double-stroke and outlined X / saltire cross
Plain lozenge/diamond and internally peaked diamond

complex_indus_specific_categories.shape_desc: Iconic Harappan rimmed-handle jar (terminal suffix sign) & hatched variants
Filled U-vessel with interior stroke or droplet
Indus human figures, horned/armed figures, and yoke-carriers (090-161)
Complex diacritic-modified fish signs (topped, roofed, finned)
Multi-element shrines, double-grid compounds, and ligatured oval/seed signs

gadd_1932.citation: C. J. Gadd (1932). 'Seals of Ancient Indian Style Found at Ur'. Proceedings of the British Academy, Vol. 18, pp. 191-210.
gadd_1932.notes: Includes Gadd No. 1 (U.7683 / BM 120573, Indus bull iconography with cuneiform 'sag-ku-zi', NOT Indus script), several uninscribed/iconographic Gulf-style seals, and a subset of circular/square seals bearing authentic Indus script.

laursen_2010.citation: Steffen Terp Laursen (2010). 'The westward transmission of Indus Valley sealing technology: origin and development of the "Gulf Type" seal and other administrative technologies in Early Dilmun, c. 2100-2000 BC'. Arabian Archaeology and Epigraphy 21: 96-134.
